passage: I'm Elizabeth. My cousin Salma watches the same video maker every evening. She copies the way she says hello and wants a bedroom like hers. Last Sunday we watched together, and Salma paused on a smiling clip. "She never has a bad day," she said. Then she frowned. "But they cut bits out, don't they? Her room video took the whole day to film, she said so at the end." She didn't say more. Later she sat with her sketchbook and drew for an hour, tearing out two pages she didn't like. I couldn't tell if she felt inspired or a little sad. Maybe both. She still watches every evening.

qa.q: What did Salma say the video maker never has?
qa.a: She said the video maker never has a bad day.

qa.q: How might Salma have felt when she frowned?
qa.a: Possibly doubtful and a little disappointed, realising the videos are edited so the smiling life may not be as perfect as it looks.

qa.q: How could Salma keep enjoying the videos in a healthy way?
qa.a: She can let the admiration inspire her own drawing while remembering that everybody's real life has hard moments too.

qa.q: How does Elizabeth see Salma's admiration?
qa.a: As something that seems inspiring and harmless, though Elizabeth admits being unable to tell whether Salma felt inspired or a little sad.

grounding: A child admires a video maker with a seemingly perfect life and starts remembering that videos are edited.
